description: Named after the legendary hypothetical "Planet X", Team Nibiru is dedicated to pushing the boundaries of deep-space discovery. Participating in the Planet X Sphere track of the NASA Space Apps Challenge, our mission is to transform complex astronomical datasets into intuitive, interactive experiences.
summary: NibiruSearch is a web workspace for exploring how the infrared sky is observed over time. Users enter coordinates or choose a challenge target, play genuine SPHEREx observations, compare selected frames, mark an interesting position and export its evidence. Background download jobs make slow archive access manageable, while cached images keep exploration responsive. Detector, wavelength, time and quality metadata stay beside the images. The tool offers source boxes, qualitative stacking and subtraction, quick-look spectral samples, noise estimates and nearby catalog searches. Optional AI-based interpretation is grounded in the supplied evidence and kept separate from measured values. To ensure data accuracy, all functions rely on mathematical algorithms, with AI only used to guide users to interpret their evidence. NibiruSearch helps the public ask reproducible questions without mistaking artifacts or wavelength differences for astronomical discoveries.
details:
The problem

SPHEREx makes the infrared sky available through observations taken at different times and wavelengths. For a member of the public, finding the relevant files, understanding which images can be compared and keeping track of the evidence can be difficult. A brighter pixel or a subtraction residual can reflect wavelength coverage, masking, background, the instrument response or noise. It does not automatically establish a moving object or a variable source.

What we built

NibiruSearch is a public-facing web application that connects archive discovery to an evidence workflow. Visitors can enter ICRS coordinates in decimal or sexagesimal form, use a name resolver, or choose Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. The viewer provides dated playback, detector and wavelength filters, date selection, zoom and pan, frame selection, comparison and candidate marking.

Persistent download jobs preserve search settings and progress. A visitor can open available cached frames while other observations download, then cancel, resume or retry the job. A manual refresh re-queries the archive for newly indexed observations while retaining cached files. Release collections are configurable; the current archive paths use DR1 and QR3, including wide/deep inventories where accessible. Weekly SIA availability can lag ingestion.

The backend reads genuine FITS cutouts, carries quality masks and reprojects images onto a common celestial grid. Blink compatibility checks constrain units, detector, release, time and approximate wavelength coverage. Selected-frame addition, subtraction and inverse-variance stacking are available. Cross-band mixtures and subtraction are clearly described as qualitative because full PSF matching, photometric normalization and calibration-systematic treatment are not implemented.

Source boxes are prepared and cached per frame using SEP. They highlight brightness peaks in usable pixels; their labels do not imply persistent tracking or confirmed star identities. Users can search SIMBAD, Gaia DR3 and AllWISE near the marked position with an adjustable radius. Catalogs retain their names, reference positions, epochs and angular offsets. We do not automatically propagate catalog positions to the observation epoch or infer identity from proximity.

At a selected position, the application can extract actual exposure-based aperture samples and estimate local random/background noise. The displayed spectrum preserves each sample's wavelength, timestamp and limitations. These samples are non-contemporaneous and use approximate WCS-WAVE calibration; they are quick-look evidence, not calibrated spectroscopy or molecular detections. A separate aggregate 102-channel cube path has been implemented.

The candidate evidence export records coordinates, observation identifiers, timestamps, wavelengths, thumbnails, measured quantities, noise estimates, source URLs, file hashes, WCS and processing limitations. Optional Gemini interpretation receives backend-built evidence and an explicit question. Structured output is validated, evidence references are checked and AI text cannot replace numerical measurements.

What we demonstrated

All five required target fields returned genuine SPHEREx cutouts. A local snapshot on 15 November 2026 at 11:31 UTC contained 34 frames for Barnard's Star, 20 for Epsilon Indi B, 24 for WISE 0855, 18 for RW Aurigae and 18 for R Draconis. These are local cache counts, not target detections, complete archive inventories or verified public-server counts. Archive errors remain visible. Software verification combines actual-data smoke checks with explicitly synthetic alignment, flux, noise and masking cases. The recorded full backend run passed 59 tests; subsequent focused job/source checks passed 13 tests, partly overlapping the earlier suite; six frontend tests passed. Browser checks exercised real images, playback, source boxes, catalog context and evidence export.

Why it matters and what comes next

NibiruSearch lowers the barrier to inspecting public infrared observations while teaching users how to question apparent changes. Its contribution is an accessible, reproducible exploration workflow, not a new astronomical discovery or a replacement for professional archive science tools. Next steps are calibrated wavelength/PSF treatment, validated spectroscopy, uncertainty-aware apparent motion and epoch-aware catalog associations.
